svg.title: Latitude from the Sun's noon altitude and declination
svg.desc: In the northern hemisphere, when the Sun is south of the zenith at noon, latitude equals 90 degrees minus the noon altitude plus the Sun's declination.

g.text: From a Noon Sun to a Latitude
Northern hemisphere, Sun south of the zenith. Declination is where the Sun stands relative to the equator that day.
or, equivalently, latitude = zenith distance + declination
At the equinox, declination is 0°, so latitude is simply 90° minus the noon altitude.
At the summer solstice, add about 23.44° (the tilt was about 23.7° in Pytheas's century).
At the winter solstice, subtract the same amount. The ±23.44° swing is the sky's expression of Earth's axial tilt,
which is also why we have seasons.
Polaris is simpler: its height is nearly your latitude, and you do not need a declination table.
In Pytheas's day, no bright star sat on the pole.
